title: Gratitude and helping
hookLine: people made to feel grateful helped a stranger more (Bartlett and DeSteno, 2006)

cards: The screen goes black. A long, dull task, nearly finished, and now the computer has frozen and it looks like the whole thing has to be done again.
Then the person sitting next to you leans over, fiddles with a cable, and the work comes back. Relief, maybe, and something warmer than relief.
That small scene was staged, in a psychology lab, to make people feel grateful on purpose. Gratitude has been on this path since day fourteen.
The researchers asked what comes next: would that feeling change what people did for someone else?

teach.b: First, the setup. Monica Bartlett and David DeSteno arranged for a participant's computer to fail near the end of a tedious task.
A partner, who was secretly part of the study, stepped in and fixed it, sparing them from starting over. Others went through the same session without being rescued. Second, the ask.
Afterward, the participants were asked to help with an unpleasant survey that would take a while. Those who had been helped, and felt grateful, spent more time helping. Third, the surprising part.
In one version of the study, the request came from a stranger, not from the person who had fixed the computer, and grateful people still helped more.
So gratitude wasn't only paying back a debt; it seemed to make people more willing to help, full stop. The researchers also checked that it wasn't just a good mood doing the work.

teach.h: A BOOK THAT STARTS WITH THANKS.
teach.b: Fourth, an old book that starts with thanks. Marcus Aurelius opens his Meditations not with a theory but with a list: what he learned from his grandfather, his mother, his teachers, his friends.
Book one is, in large part, a record of debts to people, and much of what follows turns to how to live among others.

This week followed the same thread: being the one who helps, spending on someone else, kindness spreading, a softer voice inside, and two careful looks at big claims. Gratitude sits near the start of that chain.
Something good comes in, and it moves toward the next person.

how: Some people keep a regular gratitude practice, naming people or things they are thankful for, and some religious traditions build thanks into daily prayer. Some pair thanks with a small act of help.

saying thank you so people will owe you later
feeling thankful, then more willing to help others

games.q: you're in the study. a stranger, not the person who fixed your computer, asks for help with a long, dull survey. what did grateful people tend to do?
o: say no, since the stranger hadn't helped them.
help, and for longer than people who hadn't been rescued.
games.why: gratitude seemed to widen the willingness to help, not just repay one person.

practice: Bring to mind one person who helped you, recently or long ago, and silently name what they gave, as plainly as Marcus might: from this person, patience; from that one, a ride home on a bad night.
Stay with them for a few breaths, add anyone else who comes, and notice the warmth that comes with the list, or doesn't.

wordCard.voice: Gratitude and helping. In the lab, people who felt grateful helped more, even when a stranger asked. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin for "thanks," as in the Latin liturgy's reply Deo gratias, "thanks be to God."

carryVoice: Your line: pass it on. Thanks received can turn into help given, even to someone new. Rest well.

sources.ref: Bartlett and DeSteno, "Gratitude and prosocial behavior: helping when it costs you" (Psychological Science)
